Name: reasoning_load_bearing_tokens
Title: Load-Bearing Tokens: A Mechanistic Approach to Pruning Redundant Chain-of-Thought at Inference Time
Short Hypothesis: Only a small subset of chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens are 'load-bearing'—their internal representations are causally read by later computation that produces the answer—while most CoT tokens are computationally inert filler. If we can identify load-bearing tokens mechanistically (via attention read-out and causal ablation), we can prune reasoning on the fly, cutting token generation substantially with minimal accuracy loss, without any retraining.
Related Work: Recent efficient-reasoning methods (DR.SAF; Aware First, Think Less; adaptive routing) reduce CoT length via RL, difficulty priors, or self-awareness signals, all requiring training or explicit difficulty labels. Faithfulness work (FaithCoT-Bench) studies whether CoT reflects internal computation but does not exploit this for efficiency. Prior interpretability work on CoT (e.g., attention/activation patching) explains reasoning but has not been turned into an inference-time pruning mechanism. Our proposal is distinct: we operationalize a mechanistic criterion (which CoT token representations are causally consumed downstream) into a training-free, per-instance pruning controller for efficient reasoning, bridging interpretability and efficiency.
Abstract: Long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves accuracy but generates large amounts of tokens, much of which may be computational filler that models never read back. We hypothesize that only a small fraction of CoT tokens are 'load-bearing': their hidden states are causally consumed by downstream layers when producing the final answer, while the rest can be removed without changing the answer. We test this by combining two mechanistic probes—(1) downstream attention read-out, measuring how much later positions attend to each CoT token, and (2) causal activation ablation, zeroing or knocking out a token's residual-stream contribution and measuring answer flips—to score every CoT token's causal importance. We first characterize the distribution of load-bearing tokens across math (GSM8K, MATH) and logic benchmarks and correlate with problem difficulty. We then build a training-free inference-time controller that, given a partial CoT, uses a lightweight learned linear probe (trained on offline causal scores) to predict when the model has produced enough load-bearing content, triggering early termination or skipping to the answer. We evaluate accuracy vs. tokens-generated trade-offs against length-based early exit, DR.SAF-style baselines, and full CoT. We expect substantial token reduction (30-50%) at near-equal accuracy, plus an interpretable map of what reasoning content actually matters. This yields both a practical efficiency method and mechanistic insight into CoT's true computational structure.
Experiments: 1. Load-bearing scoring: On open-weight reasoning models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), for each CoT token compute (a) aggregated downstream attention from answer-generating positions and (b) causal importance via activation ablation (mean-ablate the token's residual contribution and record whether the final answer changes). Validate that ablating low-score tokens rarely flips answers while ablating high-score tokens frequently does. 2. Characterization: Plot the fraction of load-bearing tokens per problem across GSM8K, MATH, and a logic set (e.g., ProntoQA); correlate with problem difficulty and CoT length; test whether filler concentrates in specific phrase types (hedging, restating). 3. Predictive probe: Train a lightweight linear/MLP probe on hidden states to predict, at generation time, whether sufficient load-bearing content has accumulated to answer correctly (labels from offline causal scores). 4. Inference-time controller: Use the probe to trigger early answer generation; also test a 'skip filler' variant that stops elaboration once a reasoning step is deemed inert. 5. Evaluation: Report accuracy vs. mean tokens generated (Pareto curves) against baselines: full CoT, fixed-length truncation, confidence-based early exit, and a DR.SAF-style reproduction. Metrics: accuracy, tokens generated, wall-clock latency, causal-score AUC of the probe. 6. Ablations: attention-only vs. causal-only vs. combined scoring; transfer of the probe across datasets and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Causal ablation of individual tokens may be expensive; we mitigate by sampling tokens and using cheaper attention proxies for the online controller. 2. Load-bearing structure may be diffuse rather than sparse for some models, limiting achievable savings. 3. Early termination could hurt accuracy on the hardest problems; the Pareto analysis directly quantifies this. 4. Probe may not transfer across models/datasets, requiring per-setting calibration. 5. Attention read-out is not a perfect causal signal; we validate it against direct ablation to control for this.
